questions.subtopic: 1C1 Organizational governance basics. Who establishes risk appetite
questions.question: A bank's chief risk officer drafted its risk appetite statement, which the executive committee endorsed. In the Three Lines Model, which party should an internal auditor most appropriately identify as setting risk appetite?

options.A: The bank's executive committee.
options.B: The bank's board of directors.
options.C: The bank's chief risk officer.
options.D: The bank's prudential regulator.

questions.key_concept: Risk appetite is established by the board; senior management proposes it and manages within it; internal audit assesses.
questions.pre_read: Separate three verbs: who drafts and endorses, who sets, and who assesses.
questions.correct_explanation: Setting risk appetite is a governance decision, so it belongs to the board. The IIA's 2026 statement on the Three Lines Model says boards set risk appetite, and its statement on enterprise risk management says the same. The executive committee is the closest choice because senior management usually proposes the appetite and must run the bank inside it, but drafting and endorsing a statement is different from setting the appetite.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: senior management drafts and endorses the appetite and manages within it, but it answers to the board, which sets how much risk the bank will take.
wrong_explanations.C: The chief risk officer holds a second-line role that supports, monitors and challenges. Drafting the statement is support; it does not set the appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: A regulator sets minimum rules for every bank. How much risk this bank chooses to take within those rules is its own governance decision.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a second-line role supports and drafts but does not decide, and D, because a regulator sets minimum rules, not a bank's own appetite.
Final two: B beats A because management proposes the appetite and operates within it, while setting it is the board's governance role.
Exam cue: when a question asks who sets risk appetite or direction, look to the board; management proposes and runs, and internal audit assesses.

questions.subtopic: 1C1 Organizational governance basics. Who designs and operates controls
questions.question: At an insurer, the board has set underwriting limits and the risk management function monitors them. Which party is most accurately named as responsible for designing and operating the controls over those limits?

options.A: The board that set the underwriting limits.
options.B: The risk management function.
options.C: The internal audit function.
options.D: The underwriting unit's managers.

questions.key_concept: First-line management owns the risk and designs and operates the controls; second-line functions monitor and challenge, the board directs, and internal audit assures.
questions.pre_read: Sort the four parties by verb: who sets, who runs, who monitors and who assures.
questions.correct_explanation: In The IIA's 2026 statement on the Three Lines Model, management in first-line roles owns and manages the risk, so it designs and operates the controls; here that is the underwriting unit's managers. The risk management function, the closest choice, is a second-line role: it brings expertise, monitors and challenges, as the stem says, but the risk and its controls stay with the first line. The board directs, and internal audit assures.

wrong_explanations.A: The board sets direction and limits and oversees management. Designing and operating the controls that keep to those limits is management's work.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a second-line function supports, monitors and challenges, and may advise on design, but the first line owns the risk and runs the controls.
wrong_explanations.C: The internal audit function gives independent assurance on whether the controls are well designed and working. Designing and operating them is management's work.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the board sets limits and oversees but does not run controls, and C, because internal audit assures controls that management designs and operates.
Final two: D beats B because the first line owns the risk and runs the controls, while a second-line function monitors and challenges.
Exam cue: match the verb to the party: the board sets and oversees, management owns and operates, the second line monitors, and internal audit assures.

questions.subtopic: 1C2 Culture and the control environment. Evidence of culture in practice
questions.question: An internal auditor is assessing how a retailer promotes an ethical culture. Which evidence would tell the auditor most about the culture in practice?

options.A: How managers treated staff who had raised a concern.
options.B: What senior leaders say about ethics at staff meetings.
options.C: Signed staff acknowledgments of the code.
options.D: How many concerns staff sent to the hotline last year.

questions.key_concept: Evidence must be relevant to the objective: culture in practice shows in behavior and its consequences, not in messages, documents or raw counts.
questions.pre_read: For each option, ask what it shows about how people act and what follows when they do.
questions.correct_explanation: The question is about culture in practice, so the relevant evidence is what people do and what leaders reward or punish; the treatment of staff who spoke up shows that. Standard 14.1 requires information relevant to the objective, and no Standard ranks culture evidence. The count of hotline reports, the closest choice, is behavior too, but a low count can mean a healthy culture or a fearful one.

wrong_explanations.B: Speeches show the message leaders send. Culture in practice shows in whether their actions and decisions match that message.
wrong_explanations.C: A signature shows that staff received the code. It says nothing about whether people follow it or what happens when they do not.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: reporting is behavior, but a count alone is ambiguous. Few reports can mean few problems or a fear of speaking up.

tips: Eliminate: B, because speeches show the message sent and not what is done, and C, because a signature shows that the code was received.
Final two: A beats D because a count of reports can mean trust or fear, while the treatment of those who reported shows which it is.
Exam cue: for culture in practice, prefer evidence of behavior and its consequences over messages, documents or counts that can be read two ways.

questions.subtopic: 1C2 Culture and the control environment. What an engagement risk is
questions.question: An internal auditor is starting the engagement risk assessment for a first vessel-maintenance assurance engagement at a ferry operator. Which of the following risks is the primary focus of that assessment?

options.A: Risks that the engagement will overrun its budget or deadline.
options.B: Risks that the internal auditors will reach a wrong conclusion.
options.C: Risks to the objectives of the maintenance activity under review.
options.D: Risks listed in the ferry operator's enterprise risk register.

questions.key_concept: An engagement risk assessment looks for the significant risks that threaten what the activity under review must achieve, not risks to the audit itself.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose objectives the risks threaten: the activity's, the auditors' or the whole organization's.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.2 has internal auditors understand the activity under review and identify the potentially significant risks to that activity's objectives, fraud included, then rank them for review. So an engagement risk here is a risk to vessel maintenance, such as overdue safety work. The risk of a wrong conclusion, the closest choice, is real, but supervision and due professional care manage it; the engagement risk assessment does not look for it.

wrong_explanations.A: Budget and deadline are matters for engagement resourcing and supervision. The engagement risk assessment looks at the activity under review, not at the audit project.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a wrong conclusion is a risk to the audit, managed by supervision and due professional care. The assessment identifies risks to the activity's objectives.
wrong_explanations.D: The organization's risk information is an input, but it covers everything. The engagement risk assessment narrows to the risks that threaten this activity's objectives.

tips: Eliminate: A, because budget and deadline are resourcing matters, and D, because the enterprise register is an input that covers far more than this activity.
Final two: C beats B because Standard 13.2 points the assessment at risks to the activity's objectives; the risk of a wrong conclusion is managed through supervision.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, engagement risks are whatever threatens the reviewed activity's objectives, and controls are what management does about them.

questions.subtopic: 1C2 Culture and the control environment. A significant gap behind a good outcome
questions.question: A transit agency's fare committee approved a change without the risk analysis agency policy requires, and revenue rose; an internal auditor rates the gap a significant risk. Which course best meets the Standards?

options.A: Record it and report it as an engagement finding.
options.B: Hold it unless a later fare change loses money.
options.C: Ask the committee to redo the fare decision with the analysis.
options.D: Decide whether to report it, using the function's methodologies.

questions.key_concept: A risk judged significant has to be written up and reported as a finding; only lesser risks are left to the internal auditor's judgment.
questions.pre_read: Note what the internal auditor has already concluded about the gap, then recall what follows from that.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.3 leaves no choice once a risk is judged significant: it has to be written up and reported as a finding. The good revenue result changes nothing, because significance rests on likelihood and impact, not on whether harm has happened. Deciding case by case under the function's methodologies, the closest choice, is the rule for risks that are not significant, so it does not apply here.

wrong_explanations.B: Significance is judged by likelihood and impact. A weak decision process is a risk now, whether or not a loss has yet followed.
wrong_explanations.C: Whether to revisit the decision is management's call. The internal auditor's requirement is to document the significant risk and communicate it as a finding.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: that judgment applies to risks that are not significant. Once a risk is rated significant, reporting it as a finding is a requirement.

tips: Eliminate: B, because significance does not wait for a loss, and C, because revisiting the decision is management's call while reporting the gap is the auditor's.
Final two: A beats D because discretion under the methodologies covers risks that are not significant; a significant one must be reported as a finding.
Exam cue: check how the stem rates the risk; significant means it must be reported as a finding, while a lesser risk leaves room for judgment.

questions.subtopic: 1C3 Ethics and compliance issues. A breach of the organization's own policy
questions.question: A retailer's published refund policy promises refunds within 7 days, the legal limit is 30, and an internal auditor finds refunds take about 20 days. Which view is best for the auditor to take?

options.A: Compliance is met, as refunds beat the legal limit.
options.B: The policy overstates the law and should be relaxed.
options.C: Service is slow, but no compliance criterion is breached.
options.D: The policy is a compliance criterion that is breached.

questions.key_concept: Compliance covers the organization's own policies and commitments as well as law; the law is the minimum.
questions.pre_read: List every rule in the facts that binds the retailer, then compare each with what happens.
questions.correct_explanation: Compliance, as the Standards' glossary uses the word, reaches every binding rule: law, regulation, contract and the organization's own policies and procedures. The retailer's published policy is therefore a criterion, and 20 days against a 7-day promise is a gap to evaluate as a finding. Calling it slow service with no compliance side, the closest choice, treats compliance as a matter of law alone. The law is only the minimum.

wrong_explanations.A: Meeting the 30-day legal limit satisfies the law. It does not satisfy the stricter 7-day rule the retailer has published for itself.
wrong_explanations.B: Whether to change the policy is management's decision. While the 7-day promise stands, it is the criterion that performance is measured against.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the delay is a service problem too, but compliance covers the organization's own policies, so a criterion is breached.

tips: Eliminate: A, because meeting the law does not meet the retailer's stricter policy, and B, because changing the policy is management's decision.
Final two: D beats C because compliance covers the policies an organization sets for itself, so slow refunds breach a criterion, not just a service goal.
Exam cue: when conduct is legal but breaks the organization's own policy, contract or code, it is still a compliance gap to evaluate as a finding.

questions.subtopic: 1C3 Ethics and compliance issues. An ethics concern about a senior executive
questions.question: In a pricing engagement at a drug distributor, an internal auditor finds that the chief commercial officer approved discounts for a relative's company, against the code of conduct. What is the auditor's best course?

options.A: Tell the board chair first, and the chief audit executive afterward.
options.B: Raise it with the chief audit executive under the function's methodology.
options.C: Recommend that the chief executive officer discipline the chief commercial officer.
options.D: Tell the chief executive officer, who is the officer's superior.

questions.key_concept: The internal auditor reports an ethics concern under the function's methodology; where senior management is involved, the chief audit executive should inform the board.
questions.pre_read: Ask two things: where should this concern end up, and whose step is it to take it there?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.2 requires an internal auditor who finds conduct against the organization's ethical expectations to report it under the applicable policies and procedures, and its considerations route that through the chief audit executive's methodology. They add that when senior management is involved, the chief audit executive should take the violation to the board. Telling the chair first, the closest choice, reaches the right body by going around the person whose step it is.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the board should hear of a senior executive's breach, but reporting it there is the chief audit executive's step. Going to the chair first goes around that.
wrong_explanations.C: Discipline is management's decision. The internal auditor reports facts and evidence, and those with authority decide what follows.
wrong_explanations.D: The chief executive officer is senior management too. The methodology takes the concern to the chief audit executive, who should take it to the board.

tips: Eliminate: C, because discipline is management's decision, and D, because the internal auditor follows the methodology and does not choose the recipient.
Final two: B beats A because the methodology takes the concern to the chief audit executive, who should then report a senior executive's breach to the board.
Exam cue: for an ethics concern about senior management, expect the internal auditor to tell the chief audit executive, who takes it to the board.

questions.subtopic: 1C4 Types of risk. Risk with a possible upside
questions.question: At a risk workshop for a solar developer, the facilitator removes 'subsidy may be extended' from the register because it is good news. Which treatment should an internal auditor consider most appropriate?

options.A: Leave it out until the subsidy decision is certain.
options.B: Track it as an opportunity outside risk management.
options.C: Record it as a risk with a possible upside.
options.D: Record it if it could also cause a loss.

questions.key_concept: Risk is what uncertainty may do to objectives, for better or worse, so opportunities belong inside risk management.
questions.pre_read: Test the item against two questions: is the outcome uncertain, and would it affect an objective?
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards' glossary treats risk as what uncertainty may do to objectives, for better or for worse, and The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management has threats and opportunities handled in one process. A possible subsidy extension is uncertain and bears on the developer's objectives, so it belongs in the register. Tracking it as an opportunity outside risk management, the closest choice, keeps it visible but splits off half of what risk means.

wrong_explanations.A: Once the decision is certain there is no uncertainty left to manage. Risk identification deals with events that may or may not happen.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it keeps the item visible, but risk management covers threats and opportunities together, so an upside belongs inside it.
wrong_explanations.D: It makes a possible loss the test. Risk covers favorable effects on objectives as well, so no downside is needed.

tips: Eliminate: A, because risk is about events that are still uncertain, and D, because an uncertain event needs no downside to count as a risk.
Final two: C beats B because risk covers upside as well as downside, so an opportunity is managed inside risk management, not beside it.
Exam cue: when an option treats risk as harm alone, check the definition: uncertainty can help or hurt an objective.

questions.subtopic: 1C4 Types of risk. Residual risk and controls not yet in place
questions.question: A toll-road operator's register rates cash-theft risk 'low residual', counting daily cash counts now in use and cameras approved and funded for next year. Which conclusion by an internal auditor is most accurate?

options.A: Residual risk should reflect the daily cash counts, not the cameras.
options.B: Inherent risk is overstated because cameras will reduce it.
options.C: Residual risk is fairly rated because the cameras are funded.
options.D: Residual risk equals inherent risk until the cameras work.

questions.key_concept: Residual risk is what remains after the management actions already implemented; planned controls do not reduce it yet.
questions.pre_read: Check the timing of each management action against the date of the rating.
questions.correct_explanation: In the Standards' glossary, residual risk is what is left of inherent risk once management's actions have been implemented. The daily counts are in use, so they count; cameras that are approved and funded but not installed stop no theft today. Funding, the closest choice, shows intent and a plan, and it changes the rating only when the control is in place and working.

wrong_explanations.B: Inherent risk is rated before any management action, so controls, present or future, do not change it. Cameras bear on residual risk only.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: funding shows commitment, but residual risk counts only actions already implemented. Until the cameras work, they lower nothing.
wrong_explanations.D: The daily cash counts are already in use and reduce the risk today, so residual risk is below inherent risk even without cameras.

tips: Eliminate: B, because inherent risk is rated before any controls, and D, because the daily counts in use already reduce the risk.
Final two: A beats C because residual risk reflects actions already implemented; approval and funding lower nothing until the control works.
Exam cue: when a residual rating counts a control that is planned, approved or recommended but not in place, the rating is too low.

questions.subtopic: 1C5 The risk management process. Recognizing a risk tolerance statement
questions.question: An internal auditor reads four statements in the board papers of an ambulance service. Which of the following best expresses a risk tolerance?

options.A: We accept very little risk to patient safety.
options.B: Late-response risk is rated 20 out of 25 before controls.
options.C: Vehicle breakdown losses are covered by fleet insurance.
options.D: Reach 90% of calls in 8 minutes, with 85% the floor.

questions.key_concept: Risk appetite is which risks, and how much, an organization chooses to carry; risk tolerance is how far results may stray from a target.
questions.pre_read: Look for the statement that ties an acceptable range to one objective.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk tolerance is how far results may stray from an objective and still be acceptable, so it reads as a target with a band: 90 percent, and no lower than 85. The patient-safety statement is the closest choice, but it describes risk appetite: which risks, and how much of them, the service chooses to carry, here with no measure attached. Both terms are defined in the Standards' glossary.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it states how much risk the service will take overall, with no measure. That is risk appetite, the broader of the two terms.
wrong_explanations.B: A rating made before controls describes inherent risk. It says how large the exposure is, not how much variation in results is acceptable.
wrong_explanations.C: Insurance is a risk response: it shares part of a loss with another party. It sets no acceptable range for performance.

tips: Eliminate: B, because a rating before controls is inherent risk, and C, because insurance is a response that shares a loss.
Final two: D beats A because tolerance is an acceptable range around one objective, while the safety statement is the broad appetite.
Exam cue: a broad statement of how much risk to take is appetite; a target with an acceptable range of results is tolerance.

questions.subtopic: 1C5 The risk management process. Finding the weak element of the cycle
questions.question: A glass maker's plants list all risks but rate them on separate scales, so one plant fills the board's top-ten list. Which risk management step would an internal auditor call the primary weakness?

options.A: Reporting the significant risks to the board.
options.B: Identifying the risks that threaten each plant's objectives.
options.C: Assessing the likelihood and impact of the risks.
options.D: Monitoring whether risks and responses are changing.

questions.key_concept: The IIA's 2026 risk statement lists five elements: identify, assess, manage, monitor and report; a fault in one shows up as symptoms in later ones.
questions.pre_read: Trace the visible problem back to the step where it was created.
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management names five elements: identify, assess, manage, monitor and report. Assessment is sound only when risks are rated in a consistent way, and here each plant uses its own scale, so the ratings cannot be compared. The board's list, the closest choice, is where the problem shows, but the report faithfully passes on what the ratings say: the cause sits one step earlier.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the distorted list is the visible symptom, but the report reflects the ratings it is given. The ratings are where the fault lies.
wrong_explanations.B: The facts say the plants list all their risks. Nothing suggests that risks are being missed.
wrong_explanations.D: Nothing in the facts concerns how risks or responses change over time. The problem exists on the day the ratings are made.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the plants list all their risks, and D, because nothing in the facts concerns changes in risks over time.
Final two: C beats A because the report only passes on the ratings; inconsistent scales are an assessment fault that the report then shows.
Exam cue: place each fact in the cycle of identify, assess, manage, monitor and report, and name the step where what matters is first lost, not where it shows.

questions.subtopic: 1C5 The risk management process. Risk accepted above appetite
questions.question: A museum manager accepted a fire-safety risk the chief audit executive (CAE) finds above the board's risk appetite; senior management discussed it with the CAE and declined to act. What is the CAE's best course?

options.A: Discuss the matter once more with senior management.
options.B: Escalate the matter to the board for its decision.
options.C: Accept the decision, as resolving the risk is management's job.
options.D: Schedule a fire-safety follow-up engagement for next year.

questions.key_concept: Risk accepted above appetite or tolerance: the chief audit executive must discuss it with senior management, then escalate to the board if unresolved.
questions.pre_read: Work out which conversations have already taken place and what the next step is.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 11.5 sets the order: an accepted risk above the organization's appetite or tolerance goes to senior management, and if the chief audit executive finds that senior management has left it unresolved, to the board. That point has been reached, so escalation is required. Accepting the decision, the closest choice, misreads the rule that the CAE need not resolve the risk: resolving it is not the CAE's job, but telling the board is.

wrong_explanations.A: Senior management has already discussed the matter and declined to act. Repeating the discussion delays the step the Standards now require.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the chief audit executive does not have to resolve the risk, but must still escalate a matter that senior management leaves unresolved.
wrong_explanations.D: A later engagement leaves a risk above appetite in place for a year without the board hearing of it.

tips: Eliminate: A, because senior management has already discussed the matter and declined, and D, because a later engagement leaves the board uninformed for a year.
Final two: B beats C because the chief audit executive need not resolve the risk, yet must escalate it to the board once senior management leaves it unresolved.
Exam cue: for risk accepted above appetite, find the stage reached: senior management first, then the board once the matter stays unresolved.

questions.subtopic: 1C6 Risk management across the organization. Relying on management's risk register
questions.question: The chief audit executive of a hotel group has concluded that management's risk management processes are effective. Which use of management's risk register for the internal audit plan best fits the Standards?

options.A: Adopt it unchanged as the plan's documented risk assessment.
options.B: Use it after internal audit has re-rated the risks in it.
options.C: Keep it out of the assessment to protect independence.
options.D: Rely on it as one input to internal audit's own assessment.

questions.key_concept: The plan must rest on the chief audit executive's own documented risk assessment; when to rely on management's risk information is a should.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the plan must rest on from what may feed into it.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.4 requires the plan to rest on a documented assessment of strategies, objectives and risks that the chief audit executive carries out at least yearly, informed by the board and senior management. Its considerations add that management's risk information should be relied on only where the processes behind it are judged effective, as here. So the register can feed the assessment. Adopting it unchanged, the closest choice, would let a should replace a must.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: reliance is allowed here, but the plan must still rest on a documented assessment by the chief audit executive, informed by the board and senior management.
wrong_explanations.B: Re-rating the register's risks repeats work the chief audit executive has just judged reliable. Validating the key risks is the preferred practice, not redoing the register.
wrong_explanations.C: Using management's risk information does not impair independence. The assessment must take input from senior management, and coordination is expected.

tips: Eliminate: B, because redoing the ratings repeats a process already judged effective, and C, because using management's information does not impair independence.
Final two: D beats A because the guidance on relying on management's information is a should, while basing the plan on internal audit's own documented assessment is a must.
Exam cue: an effective management process lets internal audit rely on its output as an input; it does not replace a required internal audit step.

questions.subtopic: 1C6 Risk management across the organization. Advice or design in risk assessment
questions.question: The head of risk at an agribusiness asks the internal audit function for help with this year's risk assessment refresh. Which request is most suitable for it to accept as advisory work?

options.A: Challenge the assumptions behind managers' draft risk ratings.
options.B: Set the scoring criteria managers will use to rate risks.
options.C: Rate the risks of units whose managers have not done so.
options.D: Rank the risk responses that management should fund first.

questions.key_concept: Internal audit may facilitate, advise and challenge; it must not select, prioritize or own risk responses, and it runs a process only with board-approved safeguards.
questions.pre_read: For each request, ask who would end up deciding or designing something that management should own.
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management lists challenging the assumptions behind risk assessments among advisory services: internal audit questions, and managers still own the ratings. Setting the scoring criteria, the closest choice, sounds like advice on method, but internal audit would then be designing how management rates risk, a process the same function would later audit. Rating risks for a unit does management's work, and ranking responses is a management decision.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: advising on a scoring method is fine, but setting the criteria means designing part of management's process, which goes beyond advice and impairs later assurance.
wrong_explanations.C: Rating a unit's risks is doing management's risk assessment for it. Internal audit rates risks for its own planning, not in management's place.
wrong_explanations.D: Deciding which responses get funded first is prioritizing risk responses. That is a management decision internal audit must not take.

tips: Eliminate: C, because rating a unit's risks does management's assessment for it, and D, because ranking responses for funding is management's decision.
Final two: A beats B because challenging leaves every rating with managers, while setting the criteria makes internal audit the designer of management's risk process.

Exam cue: in risk management, internal audit may facilitate, advise, challenge and assure; it must not select, prioritize or own risk responses, and running a process calls for board-approved safeguards.

questions.subtopic: 1C7 Internal control concepts and control types. A control with no stated purpose
questions.question: In a payroll engagement at a school district, an internal auditor finds a weekly sign-off whose purpose the written procedures do not explain. What is the auditor's best course?

options.A: Test whether the sign-off was performed every week.
options.B: Recommend that management remove it as a redundant control.
options.C: Ask management which risk the sign-off is meant to manage.
options.D: Leave it out of the results, which cover control gaps.

questions.key_concept: A control exists to manage a risk to an objective; find out which risk before testing it or recommending its removal.
questions.pre_read: Start from what a control is for, then ask who can say what this one is for.
questions.correct_explanation: In the Standards' glossary a control is an action taken to manage risk and make objectives more reachable, so the first question about any control is which risk it serves. Management owns the control and can answer; Standard 14.3 has internal auditors work with management on causes. Recommending removal, the closest choice, may prove right, but it is a conclusion reached before the facts: an undocumented purpose is different from no purpose.

wrong_explanations.A: Testing shows whether a step was done. Until its purpose is known, there is nothing to say whether doing it manages any risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: removal may prove right, but an undocumented purpose is different from no purpose. Management is asked before the control is called redundant.
wrong_explanations.D: Results are wider than control gaps. Chances to improve efficiency are potential findings too, and this step's purpose is still unknown.

tips: Eliminate: A, because testing performance says little until the purpose is known, and D, because results can include efficiency points as well as gaps.
Final two: C beats B because calling the sign-off redundant is a conclusion, and management has not yet been asked what it is for.
Exam cue: tie every control to a risk and an objective; where the link is unclear, ask management before testing or recommending.

questions.subtopic: 1C7 Internal control concepts and control types. A preventive control that fits the risk
questions.question: A hospital pharmacy's weekly count shows controlled-drug losses, each traced to a different pharmacist acting alone, and management asks an internal auditor for options. Which added control would best prevent further losses?

options.A: Yearly training for pharmacists on the drug policy.
options.B: A cabinet that needs two pharmacists' badges to open.
options.C: An alarm that reports cabinet openings outside shift hours.
options.D: A cabinet lock opened with a pharmacist's own personal code.

questions.key_concept: A preventive control acts before the event, and it must block the way the loss actually happens; a detective control reveals it afterward.
questions.pre_read: Sort each option by when it acts, then test what is left against how the losses occurred.
questions.correct_explanation: A preventive control stops the event; a detective control reveals it afterward. Standard 13.2's considerations name both types without defining them. The alarm acts after an opening, and training blocks nobody. Both locks act before, but each loss came from one pharmacist acting alone, and a personal code still lets one pharmacist in, so that lock, the closest choice, does not fit the risk. Two badges do. Management chooses which control to adopt.

wrong_explanations.A: Training tells pharmacists what the rules are. It does not stop a pharmacist who knows the rules and takes drugs anyway.
wrong_explanations.C: An alarm sounds protective, but it reports an opening that has already taken place. It reveals the event; it does not stop it.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: it acts before the event, but each loss came from one pharmacist acting alone, and a personal code still lets one pharmacist open the cabinet.

tips: Eliminate: A, because training states the rules but blocks nobody, and C, because an alarm reports an opening that has already happened.
Final two: B beats D because both act before a loss, but only two-badge access stops one pharmacist acting alone, which is the risk in the facts.
Exam cue: first sort controls by when they act, then check that a preventive one blocks the way the loss actually happens.

questions.subtopic: 1C7 Internal control concepts and control types. A recommendation that fits cause and cost
questions.question: An internal auditor finds duplicate supplier payments of about $3,000 a year at a grain exporter, caused by duplicate supplier records that the system accepts. Which recommendation is best to discuss with management?

options.A: A system rule that blocks a second record per supplier.
options.B: A second manual review of every supplier payment before release.
options.C: A quarterly recovery review by an outside firm.
options.D: A lower payment approval limit for accounts payable staff.

questions.key_concept: A fitting recommendation addresses the root cause at a cost in proportion to the risk; management decides and implements.
questions.pre_read: Find the cause stated in the facts, then weigh what each option would cost against the loss.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.4 has internal auditors develop recommendations that address a finding's root cause, and its considerations add that cost should be weighed against benefit. The cause is that the system accepts two records for one supplier, so a rule blocking that removes it with a one-time change. A second review of every payment, the closest choice, could stop duplicates, but it treats the symptom at a standing cost out of proportion to $3,000 a year.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it could catch duplicates before payment, but it leaves the cause in place and adds a standing cost to prevent a $3,000 loss.
wrong_explanations.C: A recovery review finds duplicates after the money has left and leaves the cause untouched. It is repeated every quarter for as long as the cause remains.
wrong_explanations.D: A lower approval limit changes who signs off payments. It does nothing about two records existing for one supplier, which is the stated cause.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a recovery review acts after payment and leaves the cause, and D, because an approval limit does not touch the duplicate records.
Final two: A beats B because blocking duplicate records removes the stated cause, while reviewing every payment treats the symptom at a standing cost out of proportion to the loss.
Exam cue: for the best recommendation, pick the option aimed at the stated root cause whose cost is in proportion to the risk.

questions.subtopic: 1C8 Control design, effectiveness and efficiency. Design gap or operating failure
questions.question: At an engineering firm, all 40 sampled expense claims carry the required supervisor approval, but the procedure sends supervisors no receipts to check. Which conclusion by an internal auditor is most accurate?

options.A: The control is effective, since sampled claims were approved.
options.B: The control is well designed but is not being operated.
options.C: The control cannot be judged until a larger sample is tested.
options.D: The control operates as written, but its design is inadequate.

questions.key_concept: Design asks whether a control would manage the risk if performed as written; operation asks whether it is performed that way.
questions.pre_read: Ask two questions in turn: is the control done as written, and could it work if done?
questions.correct_explanation: Design asks whether a control would manage the risk if performed as written; operation asks whether it is performed. Here supervisors approve every claim exactly as the procedure says, so operation is sound, but an approver who sees no receipts cannot catch a false claim: the design is inadequate. Standard 14.3's considerations treat design adequacy and effectiveness as separate judgments. Blaming the supervisors, the closest choice, misses that they followed the procedure.

wrong_explanations.A: Approval on every claim shows the step was performed. It does not show that an approval given without receipts can catch a false claim.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: it separates design from operation but reverses them. Supervisors did what the procedure says; the procedure itself gives them nothing to check.
wrong_explanations.C: More testing would repeat the same result. The evidence is already enough to judge: approvals are given, and given without receipts.

tips: Eliminate: A, because performing a step is different from managing the risk, and C, because a larger sample would repeat the same result.
Final two: D beats B because the supervisors followed the procedure exactly; the weakness is in what the procedure gives them to check.
Exam cue: when a control is performed every time yet could not catch the problem, the conclusion is a design weakness, not an operating failure.

questions.subtopic: 1C8 Control design, effectiveness and efficiency. Effective but not efficient
questions.question: At a port, three checks of container documents let no errors through but keep trucks queuing four hours; an internal auditor's tests show one check catches as much. Which conclusion is best?

options.A: The control is effective and efficient, so nothing needs reporting.
options.B: The control is effective but inefficient, which merits reporting.
options.C: The control is ineffective, since the delay harms the port.
options.D: The control is effective, and efficiency is outside assurance work.

questions.key_concept: Effective means the risk is managed; efficient means it is managed at a proportionate cost. They are separate tests.
questions.pre_read: Judge the control twice: does it manage the risk, and at what cost?
questions.correct_explanation: Effective means the risk is managed: no errors get through. Efficient means it is managed at a proportionate cost, and three checks with a four-hour queue fail that test when one check does the same job. Treating efficiency as outside assurance work is the closest choice, but Standard 9.1 lists efficient operations among the key risk areas, and Standard 14.2's considerations count efficiency improvements among potential findings.

wrong_explanations.A: Stopping every error makes the control effective. Two extra checks and a four-hour queue for the same result mean it is not efficient.
wrong_explanations.C: The control does manage its risk, since no errors get through. Delay is a cost of the control, which is an efficiency point.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the control is effective, but assurance covers efficiency as well, and chances to improve it can be reported as findings.

tips: Eliminate: A, because one check would do the same job at less cost, and C, because a control that stops every error is effective.
Final two: B beats D because a control's cost counts as well as its result: efficiency improvements can be findings, so an effective but wasteful control is worth reporting.
Exam cue: test a control twice, for whether it manages the risk and for what that costs; passing one test does not pass the other.

questions.subtopic: 1C8 Control design, effectiveness and efficiency. Using the framework the organization adopted
questions.question: A city council's board adopted an internal control framework that an internal auditor judges adequate, though sector guidance recommends a more detailed one. Which criteria best fit the Standards for the auditor's finance assurance engagement?

options.A: Criteria agreed with the finance head for this engagement.
options.B: Both frameworks, with gaps reported against each.
options.C: The framework the council already works to.
options.D: The more detailed framework that sector guidance recommends.

questions.key_concept: An adopted control framework supplies evaluation criteria; where the board and senior management have set adequate criteria, internal auditors must use them.
questions.pre_read: Ask who set the yardstick the organization measures itself by, and whether it is good enough.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.4 has internal auditors judge whether the criteria the board and senior management have established are adequate and, if they are, use them. The council's framework is adequate, so it is the yardstick. The recommended framework, the closest choice, may be a fine model, but measuring finance against a standard the council never chose sets the organization's criteria aside. Other criteria come in only when the established ones are inadequate.

wrong_explanations.A: Criteria are not negotiated with the manager of the activity when adequate ones exist. Were they inadequate, the discussion would be with the board or senior management.
wrong_explanations.B: Reporting gaps against a framework the council never adopted holds finance to a standard nobody set for it. One adequate yardstick is enough.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: recommended is not required. Adequate criteria set by the board must be used; a more detailed model does not displace them.

tips: Eliminate: A, because criteria are not negotiated with the activity's manager when adequate ones exist, and B, because gaps against a framework nobody adopted have no standing.
Final two: C beats D because adequate criteria established by the board must be used; a more detailed model that guidance recommends does not replace them.
Exam cue: for criteria, first ask whether the board and senior management have set adequate ones; if so, internal auditors use those.

questions.subtopic: 1C1 Organizational governance basics. Governance among four definitions
questions.question: The chief executive officer of a rail operator tells an internal auditor that governance is 'the executive team's management system'. Which description best matches governance as the Standards define it?

options.A: The way executives carry out strategy and answer to the board.
options.B: The structures and processes a board sets up to direct and oversee.
options.C: The rules and routines that hold risks inside the risk tolerance.
options.D: The process for finding, weighing and handling events that affect objectives.

questions.key_concept: Governance is the board's: the structures and processes it puts in place to direct and oversee the organization. Management works inside them.
questions.pre_read: Each option describes something real. Ask which body the Standards name as putting governance in place.
questions.correct_explanation: In the Standards' glossary, governance belongs to the board: it is the set of arrangements the board puts in place to steer the organization toward its objectives and keep watch on its progress. Senior management, the closest choice, carries out the strategy and answers to the board, so it works inside governance and does not author it. The other two options describe control processes and risk management.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: this describes senior management, which carries out strategy and answers to the board. Management works inside governance; the board puts governance in place.
wrong_explanations.C: This matches the glossary's control processes: the policies and activities that keep risks inside what the organization will tolerate.
wrong_explanations.D: This is risk management: the work of spotting, sizing up and dealing with whatever could affect objectives.

tips: Eliminate: C, because rules and routines that keep risks within tolerance are control processes, and D, because finding and handling events that affect objectives is risk management.
Final two: B beats A because the glossary gives governance to the board; executives carry out strategy inside the structures the board sets up.
Exam cue: when asked what governance is, look for the board as its author. A description of running the organization is management, not governance.

questions.question: A new chief audit executive is building an understanding of governance at a port authority before drafting the internal audit plan. Which step is most accurately called a requirement of the Standards?

options.B: Identify which governance frameworks the port has put in place.

options.D: Consider how the board, management and assurance providers coordinate.

wrong_explanations.C: Reading board charters, agendas and minutes is a may: one optional way to gain insight into the board's role.

tips: Eliminate: A, because adopting a framework is the board's and management's decision and no standard requires the recommendation, and C, because reviewing board papers is an optional may.

questions.subtopic: 1C2 Culture and the control environment. A decision process that meets its criteria
questions.question: A cooperative's policy lets one officer set prices alone; an internal auditor's assurance engagement judged that policy adequate as criteria and found every decision complied. Which treatment do the Standards most clearly require?

options.A: State in the conclusion that the decision process is effective.
options.B: Report the single decision-maker as a low-priority finding.
options.C: Recommend that management add a second approver for price changes.
options.D: Leave the process out of the conclusion, as nothing failed.

questions.key_concept: A finding is a gap between criteria and condition. With adequate criteria met, the assurance conclusion says the process is effective.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a finding needs before choosing: a criterion, and a condition that falls short of it.
questions.correct_explanation: Under Standard 14.2 a potential finding arises only where the condition departs from the criteria, and internal auditors who see no such gap must give assurance in the conclusion that the processes are effective; Standard 14.5 adds that conclusions acknowledge effective processes. A low-priority finding, the closest choice, has no gap behind it: the policy the auditor judged adequate allows one officer to decide, and every decision complied.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: a finding needs a gap between criteria and condition. The adequate policy allows one decision-maker and was met, so there is no finding to report.
wrong_explanations.C: A second approver would be a stricter criterion. The auditor may suggest it as an improvement, but nothing requires it: adequate criteria must be used, and they were met.
wrong_explanations.D: Assurance conclusions do not go silent when nothing failed: they must acknowledge processes that are effective.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a stricter criterion may be suggested but is not required, and D, because an assurance conclusion must acknowledge processes that are effective.
Final two: A beats B because a finding is a gap between criteria and condition, and here the adequate policy was met in every decision.
Exam cue: fewer approvers is not a finding in itself. Compare the condition with adequate criteria; where they match, expect a conclusion that the process is effective.

questions.subtopic: 1C2 Culture and the control environment. Telling a control from a risk and an objective
questions.question: An internal auditor is building a risk and control matrix for vaccine storage at a clinic. Which entry best belongs in the column for controls?

options.A: A nurse reads and logs the fridge temperature every shift.
options.B: Vaccine stock must stay between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius.
options.C: A fridge failure overnight could spoil the vaccine stock.
options.D: Spoiled vaccine stock would cost roughly $9,000 to replace.

questions.key_concept: A control is an action taken to manage a risk. The matrix keeps it apart from the objective, the risk and the effect.
questions.pre_read: Sort each entry: what must be achieved, what could go wrong, what is done about it, what it would cost.
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards' glossary defines a control as an action that management or others take to manage risk and make objectives more likely to be met, and Standard 13.2's considerations have the engagement risk assessment set out objectives, risks and the controls meant to manage each. Logging the temperature is something done about the risk. The temperature range, the closest choice, states the result to be achieved: an objective or a criterion, not an action.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the temperature range says what must be achieved. It is the objective, or a criterion to test against, not something done to manage the risk.
wrong_explanations.C: A fridge failing overnight is what could go wrong: an event that threatens the objective. That is the risk.
wrong_explanations.D: The replacement cost is the effect if the risk happens. It helps rate the risk's impact.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a fridge failure that could spoil stock is the risk, and D, because the replacement cost is the effect used to rate impact.
Final two: A beats B because a control is an action taken to manage a risk, while the temperature range states the result to be achieved.
Exam cue: in a risk and control matrix, a control is something done about a risk. A line that only states the result wanted is an objective or a criterion.

questions.subtopic: 1C2 Culture and the control environment. Challenge of decisions and reporting lines
questions.question: At a lender, the credit-risk team that challenges large loan proposals reports to the head of lending, who approves those loans. Which reading by an internal auditor is most accurate?

options.A: The challenge is credible: the reviewers are credit-risk specialists.
options.B: The challenge is credible: the reviewers are separate from loan officers.
options.C: The challenge is weakened: the reviewers' reporting line limits their objectivity.
options.D: The challenge is weakened: second-line roles lack internal audit's independence.

questions.key_concept: Second-line challenge is credible when reviewers are organizationally separate from the decision owner; reporting to that owner limits their objectivity.
questions.pre_read: Look at who the reviewers answer to, and whose decisions they are meant to question.
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on the Three Lines Model expects second-line roles to be objective enough for credible challenge, and links that to separation and distance from the decision owner's hierarchy. The reviewers answer to the person whose approvals they question. The closest choice blames the second line's place in management, but the statement treats that as normal: such roles are part of management and can still challenge credibly when separate from the first line.

wrong_explanations.A: Specialist skill makes the reviewers competent. It does not make them objective toward a manager who approves the loans and also directs their work.
wrong_explanations.B: Separation from the loan officers helps, but the reviewers still sit under the approver, the decision owner they are meant to challenge.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: every second-line role lacks internal audit's independence, yet a well-placed one challenges credibly. What weakens this team is reporting to the approver it challenges.

tips: Eliminate: A, because specialist skill is competence and not objectivity, and B, because the reviewers remain under the approver whose decisions they question.
Final two: C beats D because D would fault every second-line team. The statement ties a reviewer's objectivity to distance from the decision owner; these reviewers report to that owner.
Exam cue: to judge whether challenge is real, trace the challenger's reporting line. If it ends at the person being challenged, objectivity is limited.

questions.subtopic: 1C3 Ethics and compliance issues. A plan with no ethics program engagement
questions.question: An insurer's internal audit plan has no ethics program engagement this year: the documented risk assessment considered one and ranked other areas higher. Which view by an internal auditor is most accurate?

options.A: The plan falls short: the Standards name ethics programs for coverage.
options.B: The plan conforms: the board, which approves it, decides its coverage.
options.C: The plan falls short: another provider should assure a risk left out.
options.D: The plan conforms: the omission was a decision made on risk.

questions.key_concept: The plan must consider coverage of the compliance and ethics programs; whether an engagement goes in this year follows the risk assessment.
questions.pre_read: Check the strength of the duty: does the plan have to cover the program, or consider covering it?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.4 requires the internal audit plan to consider coverage of the compliance and ethics programs and to rest on a documented risk assessment. Here the assessment considered an engagement and ranked other areas higher, so that requirement is met. The closest choice reads 'consider coverage' as 'cover'. Had the program been rated high risk, the chief audit executive would also have to tell the board and senior management why no engagement is planned.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the Standards name ethics programs among the areas whose coverage the plan must consider. Considering is not covering; risk decides which engagements the plan holds.
wrong_explanations.B: The board does approve the plan, but approval is not the test here. What shows that coverage was considered is the documented risk assessment behind the choice.
wrong_explanations.C: Nothing requires another provider to assure each area the plan leaves out. Coverage by other providers is something the chief audit executive should consider, not a test the plan fails.

tips: Eliminate: B, because board approval does not show that coverage was considered, and C, because coverage by other providers is something to consider, not a test the plan fails.
Final two: D beats A because Standard 9.4 requires the plan to consider coverage of the ethics program; the documented risk assessment decides whether an engagement goes in.
Exam cue: read the verb in a planning duty. 'Consider coverage' is met by a documented, risk-based decision; it does not put the area in every year's plan.

questions.subtopic: 1C3 Ethics and compliance issues. Helping present the code of conduct
questions.question: A utility's chief audit executive assigns an internal auditor to co-present the code of conduct at one staff induction, as the ethics officer asked. Which view of the assignment is most accurate?

options.A: Improper: internal audit would be championing a program it may later assess.
options.B: Proper: internal auditors are required to promote an ethics-based culture.
options.C: Proper, provided internal audit gives no later assurance on ethics.
options.D: Proper, once the board has approved it as a nonaudit role.

questions.key_concept: Internal auditors must promote an ethics-based culture. Giving training is advisory work with no management responsibility, and Standard 2.2 lets assurance follow it with safeguards.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether presenting the code once makes the auditor own or decide anything in the ethics program.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 1.2 makes promoting an ethics-based culture part of every internal auditor's job, and the glossary lists providing training among advisory services, which carry no management responsibility. The auditor presents once; the ethics officer still owns the program. The closest choice bars later assurance, which Standard 2.2 does not: assurance may follow advisory work when the chief audit executive confirms objectivity is not impaired and staffs the engagement so each auditor's objectivity is managed.

wrong_explanations.A: Presenting the code once is advice, with no management responsibility taken on. Assurance may still follow, under the safeguards Standard 2.2 sets for work after advice.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: advisory work does not bar later assurance. The chief audit executive must confirm it left objectivity unimpaired and staff the engagement so each auditor's objectivity is managed.
wrong_explanations.D: Board approval and charter safeguards are for roles beyond internal auditing. Training is an advisory service, which the board hears of through normal reporting.

tips: Eliminate: A, because presenting the code once is advice with no management responsibility, and D, because board approval is the safeguard for roles beyond internal auditing.

Final two: B beats C because promoting an ethics-based culture is required, and assurance may follow advisory work once the chief audit executive confirms objectivity and staffs the engagement to manage it.
Exam cue: internal audit supports the ethics framework by promoting, assessing and reporting. Decline or add safeguards only when the auditor would own, run or decide something.

questions.subtopic: 1C4 Types of risk. Managing what triggers reputational harm
questions.question: A hotel group's register lists the reputational risk 'loss of guest trust'; complaint records show food-safety lapses usually trigger it. Which response should an internal auditor expect to reduce its likelihood most?

options.A: A media statement kept ready for any food-safety incident.
options.B: Insurance cover for bookings lost after a food-safety incident.
options.C: Daily kitchen checks on food safety, reviewed by a manager.
options.D: A survey asking each departing guest about food and cleanliness.

questions.key_concept: Reputational harm usually follows another risk event. Its likelihood falls when the event that triggers it is controlled; communication deals with the aftermath.
questions.pre_read: Separate two things: what makes guests lose trust, and what the group does after trust is lost.
questions.correct_explanation: The glossary separates likelihood, the chance that an event occurs, from impact, its effect, and Standard 11.5's considerations list harm to reputation among the impacts that may follow when risks exceed the risk appetite: reputation suffers through some other event. The records name the trigger, so checks on kitchen food safety lower the chance that trust is lost at all. A media statement, the closest choice, works after an incident: it limits damage, not likelihood.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a prepared statement helps after an incident and can limit the damage. It does nothing to make the incident, or the lost trust, less likely.
wrong_explanations.B: Insurance pays part of the financial loss once bookings fall. Trust is still lost, and the event is just as likely.
wrong_explanations.D: A survey reveals a problem after guests have met it. It detects; it does not lower the chance of the lapse.

tips: Eliminate: B, because insurance only shares the financial loss afterward, and D, because a survey finds out after guests were affected.
Final two: C beats A because checks on the trigger lower the likelihood of lost trust, while a media statement only limits the impact afterward.
Exam cue: when a question asks what lowers likelihood, look for the control over the event that triggers the loss. Responses that act after the event change the impact.

questions.subtopic: 1C4 Types of risk. Reading reliance on controls from two ratings
questions.question: A cocoa cooperative's register scores each risk out of 25 before and after management's actions. For which risk should an internal auditor conclude the cooperative depends on its controls the most?

options.A: Bean theft from depots: 20 before, 15 after.
options.B: Late export paperwork: 12 before, 10 after.
options.C: Scale tampering by cocoa buyers: 9 before, 3 after.
options.D: Fire at the main warehouse: 20 before, 5 after.

questions.key_concept: The gap between inherent and residual risk shows how much the organization leans on its controls; a large gap is a reason to test them.
questions.pre_read: Two numbers per risk: before management's actions and after. Which comparison shows what the controls are carrying?
questions.correct_explanation: By the glossary, inherent risk is the exposure with no management actions and residual risk is the part left after them, so the difference is what the actions are credited with. Fire falls from 20 to 5: fifteen points rest on controls working, the largest fall of the four. Bean theft, the closest choice, has the highest score after controls, which shows where the most exposure remains, not where controls are relied on most.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: 15 is the highest score after controls, so theft leaves the most exposure. But its controls remove only 5 points, far fewer than for fire.
wrong_explanations.B: The rating moves from 12 to 10. Controls are credited with 2 points, the least reliance of the four.
wrong_explanations.C: Tampering falls by 6 points from a low start. The reliance is real but much smaller than the 15 points credited for fire.

tips: Eliminate: B, because its controls are credited with only 2 points, and C, because a 6-point fall from a low score is modest reliance.
Final two: D beats A because reliance on controls is the fall from inherent to residual, 15 points for fire, while theft's 15 is what remains.
Exam cue: read what the question measures. Highest residual shows where exposure remains; the largest fall from inherent to residual shows where controls matter most.

questions.subtopic: 1C5 The risk management process. An accepted risk that happened
questions.question: A farm lender accepted flood risk at two valley branches, within its board's risk appetite; a flood then closed both for a week. Which conclusion by an internal auditor is most accurate?

options.A: No failure is shown: carrying this risk was a choice within limits.
options.B: Risk management failed: a risk accepted above appetite must be escalated.
options.C: Risk management failed: effective responses keep losses within tolerance.
options.D: No failure is shown: both branches were open again after a week.

questions.key_concept: Risk management aims at reasonable assurance, not at removing risk. A risk accepted knowingly within appetite can still happen without the process having failed.
questions.pre_read: Judge the decision by what was known and allowed when it was made, not by what happened next.
questions.correct_explanation: The glossary gives risk management the aim of reasonable assurance that objectives are achieved, and describes risk appetite as how much risk, and of what kinds, an organization chooses to take on. Accepting flood risk inside that appetite was a legitimate response, so the flood alone shows no failure. The closest choice turns an aim into a promise: responses are meant to keep results within tolerance, but nothing here shows a tolerance breached.

wrong_explanations.B: The rule is real, but it applies to risk accepted above appetite or tolerance. This risk was accepted within appetite, so nothing called for escalation.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: keeping results within tolerance is the aim of responses, not a guarantee. A risk accepted within appetite remains a risk, and no breach of tolerance is shown.
wrong_explanations.D: A quick reopening is a good outcome, but outcomes do not prove a sound process. The test is whether the acceptance sat within appetite when made.

tips: Eliminate: B, because escalation is for risk accepted above appetite, which this was not, and D, because a quick recovery is an outcome and not the test.
Final two: A beats C because risk management gives reasonable assurance, not a guarantee; a risk knowingly accepted within appetite can still happen.
Exam cue: a loss does not prove risk management failed, and a lucky escape does not prove it worked. Compare the decision with appetite and tolerance.

questions.subtopic: 1C5 The risk management process. A result below target but within tolerance
questions.question: A payments firm targets 99.9% uptime with a tolerance floor of 99.5%; uptime was 99.7%, which the operations manager accepted without action. Which response by the chief audit executive fits the Standards best?

options.A: Discuss the manager's acceptance of the shortfall with senior management.
options.B: Escalate the manager's acceptance of the shortfall to the board.
options.C: Treat the result as inside the range the firm accepts.
options.D: Treat the result as acceptable because the manager owns that risk.

questions.key_concept: Risk tolerance is the acceptable variation around a target. The duty to raise accepted risk starts only when appetite or tolerance is exceeded.
questions.pre_read: Place 99.7% between the two numbers the firm has set before deciding whether anything needs raising.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 11.5 applies only when the chief audit executive judges that management has accepted more risk than the organization's appetite or tolerance allows; the glossary treats tolerance as the acceptable band of results around an objective. At 99.7%, uptime is below target but above the 99.5% floor, so nothing needs raising. Discussion with senior management, the closest choice, is the first step only once that line has been crossed.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: this is the first required step under Standard 11.5, but only for risk accepted beyond appetite or tolerance. A result inside the tolerance band does not trigger it.
wrong_explanations.B: The board hears of accepted risk when senior management has not resolved it. Nothing here exceeds tolerance, so there is nothing to escalate.
wrong_explanations.D: The manager does own the risk, but ownership is not the yardstick. The firm's tolerance is; acceptance beyond it would have to be raised.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the board comes in only after senior management leaves an excessive risk unresolved, and D, because owning a risk does not set the yardstick; the firm's tolerance does.
Final two: C beats A because discussion with senior management is required only for risk accepted beyond appetite or tolerance; 99.7% sits inside the firm's stated band.
Exam cue: before choosing between discuss and escalate, check the trigger. Below target is not the test; outside appetite or tolerance is.

questions.subtopic: 1C5 The risk management process. Four responses as a register records them
questions.question: An internal auditor is assessing how a retailer's risk register records four risk responses. Which entry is recorded least soundly?

options.A: Currency swings: mostly hedged; residual risk rated low.
options.B: Customer data breach: insured; residual risk recorded as nil.
options.C: Stock shrinkage: accepted within appetite; the decision is on record.
options.D: Loss-making overseas branch: closed; residual risk recorded as nil.

questions.key_concept: Residual risk is what remains after management's actions. Insurance covers part of a loss and leaves the event possible; ending an activity removes its risk.
questions.pre_read: Two entries claim nothing is left. For each, ask whether the event could still happen and who would still answer for it.
questions.correct_explanation: By the glossary, residual risk is the exposure still left after management has acted on a risk. Insurance pays toward a loss within its terms, but a breach can still happen, uncovered costs stay with the retailer, and it still answers to its customers, so 'nil' overstates the response. The closed branch, the closest choice, also records nil, but there the activity that carried the risk has ended.

wrong_explanations.A: Hedging most of the exposure and rating the remainder low is consistent: some risk is left and the entry says so.
wrong_explanations.C: Accepting a risk within appetite is a legitimate response, and recording the decision is good practice. Nothing here is unsound.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: nil is plausible here because closing the branch ends the activity that carried the risk. Insurance leaves the activity, and the event, in place.

tips: Eliminate: A, because a hedged exposure with a low residual rating is consistent, and C, because acceptance within appetite, on record, is a legitimate response.
Final two: B beats D because insurance pays toward a loss while the breach can still happen, whereas closing the branch ends the activity itself.
Exam cue: be wary of 'transferred, so no risk'. Sharing a loss leaves the event, the uncovered part and the accountability with the organization.

questions.subtopic: 1C5 The risk management process. Judging responses against tolerance and cost
questions.question: A freight firm tolerates yearly cargo-theft losses up to $50,000 per depot; untreated, each depot expects to lose $80,000. Which depot's response should an internal auditor assess as fitting the risk best?

options.A: Sucre tracks its trucks: costs $10,000; expected loss $30,000.
options.B: Oruro accepts the risk: no cost; expected loss $80,000.
options.C: Tarija escorts its trucks: costs $200,000; expected loss $5,000.
options.D: Uyuni insures with a $100,000 deductible: costs $15,000; retained loss $80,000.

questions.key_concept: A response fits when residual risk falls within tolerance at a cost in proportion to the risk; the lowest residual risk is not automatically best.
questions.pre_read: Apply two tests in order: is the remaining loss within $50,000, and does the cost make sense for what it saves?
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 14.4's considerations have internal auditors weigh a recommendation or action plan by a cost-benefit analysis and by whether it deals with the risk in line with the organization's risk tolerance; the same two tests fit any risk response. Tracking cuts the expected loss from $80,000 to $30,000, inside tolerance, for $10,000. Escorts, the closest choice, also meet tolerance, but $200,000 a year buys a $75,000 reduction. Accepting and insuring both leave $80,000.

wrong_explanations.B: Acceptance is legitimate only within tolerance. An expected loss of $80,000 is above the $50,000 the firm tolerates.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the loss falls to $5,000, well inside tolerance, but the escorts cost $200,000 a year to save $75,000. The cost is out of proportion to the risk.
wrong_explanations.D: With a $100,000 deductible the depot still bears the expected $80,000 itself, so the retained loss stays above tolerance despite the premium.

tips: Eliminate: B, because an accepted loss of $80,000 is above tolerance, and D, because the deductible leaves the same $80,000 with the depot.
Final two: A beats C because both meet the $50,000 tolerance, but tracking does so for $10,000 while escorts cost more than the loss they prevent.
Exam cue: judge a risk response twice. First against appetite and tolerance, then against cost; the strongest control is not the best if it costs more than the risk.

questions.subtopic: 1C6 Risk management across the organization. What an adopted framework gives the auditor
questions.question: Managers of a pension administrator adopted a recognized risk management framework last year. What is the primary thing the adoption gives an internal auditor assessing the risk management process?

options.A: Evidence that managers now handle risk in one consistent way.
options.B: A basis for relying on managers' risk ratings in the plan.
options.C: A common risk language for managers across the administrator.
options.D: A reference point for judging how the process is designed and run.

questions.key_concept: An adopted risk management framework supplies structure, a common language and criteria. Adoption does not show that risk management is effective.
questions.pre_read: Adopting a framework is a decision. Ask what a decision can prove, and what still has to be tested.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 13.2 lists applicable frameworks among the information internal auditors must gather, as criteria for evaluating whether processes are effective, and Standard 13.4's considerations name frameworks among authoritative criteria. So the adopted framework gives the auditor the yardstick: what good risk management should look like here. Evidence of consistent practice, the closest choice, comes only from comparing what managers actually do with that yardstick; adoption shows intent, not results.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: adoption shows what managers intend. Whether they now handle risk consistently is shown by comparing practice with the framework, the assessment still to be done.
wrong_explanations.B: Relying on management's risk information should follow a conclusion that the risk management processes are effective. Adopting a framework is not that conclusion.
wrong_explanations.C: A common language is a real benefit, but it is what the framework gives management. For the auditor assessing the process, its main use is as criteria.

tips: Eliminate: B, because reliance on managers' ratings should follow a conclusion that the process is effective, and C, because a common language is the framework's benefit to management, not the auditor's main use of it.
Final two: D beats A because a framework states what good looks like, the criteria; evidence of what managers do comes from testing practice against it.
Exam cue: 'we adopted a framework' answers which yardstick applies, never whether the organization measures up. Expect the auditor to test practice against it.

questions.subtopic: 1C6 Risk management across the organization. A process that runs but is not used
questions.question: A logistics group's units rate risks on one approved scale and escalate them as required, and its major investment papers do not mention risk. Which conclusion by an internal auditor is most accurate?

options.A: Effective: ratings and escalation both follow the approved method.
options.B: Effective: internal audit assesses the process, not managers' business decisions.
options.C: Not effective: risk management is judged by use, not by ratings alone.
options.D: Not effective: major investments need the risk function's approval first.

questions.key_concept: Assessing risk management covers design, operation and use: a process that runs as designed is not fully effective until risk information shapes decisions.
questions.pre_read: Three questions: is the process well set up, is it followed, and does anyone decide differently because of it?
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management describes assurance over it as covering whether risks are identified, assessed and escalated reliably and also whether decision-makers use the risk information. Here the first parts work, but major investment decisions are made without reference to risk. The closest choice stops at ratings and escalation: a process that is followed yet changes no decision has not done its job.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: sound ratings and escalation show the process is followed. Effectiveness also asks whether risk information is used, and the investment papers suggest it is not.
wrong_explanations.B: True as far as it goes: the decisions are management's. But whether risk information feeds them is part of the process that assurance over risk management evaluates.
wrong_explanations.D: Management decides on investments; the risk function supports and challenges. The gap is that the papers ignore risk information, not that an approval is missing.

tips: Eliminate: B, because whether decisions use risk information is part of the process being assessed, and D, because the risk function challenges while management decides.
Final two: C beats A because following the method shows the process operates; with no investment paper mentioning risk, its output is not used where decisions are made.
Exam cue: for risk management, check design, operation and use. A register kept perfectly that no decision refers to is a record, not risk management.
