questions.subtopic: 1C2 Culture and the control environment. Culture as part of governance
questions.question: Preparing the internal audit plan at a property developer, the chief audit executive (CAE) hears the chief operating officer call culture HR's matter, outside the governance the CAE must understand. Which reply is most accurate?

options.A: Not so: culture enters the plan once HR reports show a problem.
options.B: Agreed for planning, though engagements may still comment on culture.
options.C: Not so: culture is governance, so internal audit should own it.
options.D: Not so: promoting an ethical culture is part of its governance.

questions.key_concept: Culture is part of governance: the chief audit executive must consider how the organization promotes an ethical culture; management owns the programs shaping it.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether culture is part of governance at all times, and who owns the program that shapes it.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 9.1 lists the way an organization promotes an ethical culture among the governance matters the chief audit executive must consider to build the strategy and plan, and Standard 9.4 keeps the plan current as culture changes. HR may run programs that shape culture, and senior management owns them. The closest choice leaves culture to single engagements, but the requirement applies when the plan is built.

wrong_explanations.A: Considering how an ethical culture is promoted is part of understanding governance for every plan, not a step that waits for HR to report a problem.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: engagements may assess culture, but considering how an ethical culture is promoted is required when the chief audit executive builds the strategy and plan.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal auditors must promote an ethics-based culture, but owning the program would put internal audit in management's role and weaken its later assurance on it.

tips: Eliminate: A, because considering culture does not wait for HR to report a problem, and C, because promoting a culture is not owning its program.
Final two: D beats B because considering how an ethical culture is promoted is part of understanding governance for the plan, not only a topic engagements may touch.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, culture is part of governance: internal audit considers and assesses it, and management owns the programs that shape it.

questions.subtopic: 1C6 Risk management across the organization. A risk process that leaves out major units
questions.question: A food group's risk policy covers head office and its plants, which apply it fully; two foreign subsidiaries, 40% of sales, lie beyond it. Which conclusion by an internal auditor is most accurate?

options.A: Effective: each unit the policy covers applies it as written.
options.B: Not effective in design: it leaves out units holding major risks.
options.C: Effective, with the subsidiaries' risks a matter for their own managers.
options.D: Not effective in operation: the subsidiaries' risks go unmanaged.

questions.key_concept: Risk management is judged for the whole organization: a process that works where it applies but leaves out major units is inadequately designed.
questions.pre_read: Ask first whether the process reaches every part of the group, then whether it works where it reaches.
questions.correct_explanation: The IIA's 2026 statement on enterprise risk management treats it as one joined-up effort across the whole organization, and its assurance asks both whether the process is well designed and whether it works. A policy that never reaches units holding 40% of sales leaves their risks outside the process by design. The closest choice calls this an operating failure, but the gap is in what the policy covers.

wrong_explanations.A: The covered units work well, but risk management is judged for the organization as a whole. Units holding 40% of sales are left out, so the design falls short.
wrong_explanations.C: The subsidiaries' risks are the group's risks, and the board needs one view of them. Their own managers may run the process, but the group's process should reach them.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: unmanaged subsidiary risks would be an effect, and the stem does not show it. What fails is the policy's reach, a gap in design, not in operation.

tips: Eliminate: A, because risk management is judged for the whole group, not unit by unit, and C, because the subsidiaries' risks are the group's risks.
Final two: B beats D because the policy never reached the subsidiaries; that is a gap in design, and an effect seen there would not make it an operating failure.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about risk management, check coverage before operation: a process that runs well but misses major units has a design gap.

questions.subtopic: 1C5 The risk management process. A hub below its floor while the group is within appetite
questions.question: A courier's on-time floor is 92% per hub, and group risk is within the board's appetite; one hub's manager accepted 88% last quarter, planning no change. Which view by an internal auditor is most accurate?

options.A: No matter to raise: group risk stays inside the board's appetite.
options.B: No matter to raise: the hub's manager owns that risk and accepted it.
options.C: A matter to raise: the hub's result falls outside its risk tolerance.
options.D: A matter to raise: the per-hub floor is the board's risk appetite.

questions.key_concept: A floor around one objective is a risk tolerance. Risk accepted beyond it is a Standard 11.5 matter, even while overall risk stays within appetite.
questions.pre_read: Name each yardstick first: a measured floor for one objective is a tolerance, and the board's appetite covers risk overall. Either can be exceeded alone.
questions.correct_explanation: The 92% floor is an acceptable variation in performance for one objective, which the glossary calls risk tolerance. Standard 11.5 covers risk that management accepts beyond the organization's appetite or tolerance, so the hub's 88% goes to the chief audit executive, who should raise it with the manager first and must then discuss it with senior management if unresolved. The closest choice measures against appetite alone; staying within appetite does not cancel an exceeded tolerance.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: appetite is one yardstick, set for risk overall. Standard 11.5 also covers risk accepted beyond tolerance, and the per-hub floor is a tolerance.
wrong_explanations.B: Owning a risk lets the manager act on it; it does not set aside the courier's floor. Acceptance beyond tolerance is what Standard 11.5 asks to be raised.
wrong_explanations.D: The verdict fits, the reason does not: a floor on one objective's performance is a tolerance, and group risk sits within the board's appetite. Tolerance is the limit passed.

tips: Eliminate: B, because owning a risk does not let a manager set aside the organization's floor, and D, because a floor on one objective is a tolerance, not the board's appetite.
Final two: C beats A because Standard 11.5 is triggered by risk accepted beyond appetite or tolerance; the hub's floor is a tolerance, and staying within appetite does not cancel it.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, a measured floor or band around one objective is risk tolerance; check it apart from the board's appetite before deciding nothing needs raising.

questions.subtopic: 1C3 Ethics and compliance issues. No policy yet on where internal auditors send concerns
questions.question: No policy at a mining cooperative yet says where internal auditors should send ethics concerns or legal violations; management's policy is a year away. Meanwhile, what should the chief audit executive best do?

options.A: Set the function's own steps for routing such matters for now.
options.B: Ask the ethics officer where to route each matter as it arises.
options.C: Send each matter to the board until management's policy is issued.
options.D: Advise management on what its coming policy should say.

questions.key_concept: Where policy is silent on routing ethics concerns or legal violations, internal auditors follow a methodology the chief audit executive sets for the function.
questions.pre_read: Separate the organization's policy, which management writes and owns, from internal audit's methodology, which the chief audit executive sets for the function's own work.
questions.correct_explanation: Internal auditors must report ethics concerns under applicable policies and send legal violations to those with authority to act. Where policy is silent, Standard 1.3's considerations let the chief audit executive set auditors' steps, Standard 1.2's ask for a methodology for ethical issues, discussed with the board and senior management, and Standard 9.3 requires methodologies guiding conformance. The closest choice, advising on management's policy, is allowed but leaves auditors with no route for a year.

wrong_explanations.B: An ethics officer is the route where policy names one. None does here, so the considerations look to the chief audit executive's methodology, not one officer's case-by-case view.
wrong_explanations.C: Standard 1.2's considerations send conduct by senior management or the board chair to the board. Sending every matter there bypasses the managers with authority to act on the rest.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: advising on a new policy is allowed advisory work, and the policy stays management's. It does not tell the function's auditors where to send concerns this year.

tips: Eliminate: B, because one officer's case-by-case view replaces set steps, and C, because sending every matter to the board bypasses the managers with authority to act on most of them.
Final two: A beats D because advising on management's future policy leaves auditors with no route now; the chief audit executive's own methodology fills the gap until policy does.
Exam cue: on CIA questions, when policy is silent on how internal auditors should handle a matter, look first to the function's own methodology, which the chief audit executive sets.

questions.subtopic: 1C2 Culture and the control environment. Behavior that breaks no rule
questions.question: Reviewing an airline's behavioral risk process, which tracks only misconduct and policy breaches, an internal auditor finds junior engineers rarely question senior engineers' repair calls. Which view is most accurate?

options.A: Complete: behavioral risk means misconduct and breaches of policy.
options.B: Incomplete: habits that breach nothing can still threaten objectives.
options.C: Incomplete, if a survey shows the pattern runs across every hangar.
options.D: Complete: engineers can raise any repair doubts through the safety hotline.

questions.key_concept: Behavioral risk is behavior at odds with the organization's objectives, so a process that tracks only misconduct and policy breaches is incomplete by design.
questions.pre_read: Recall how the Organizational Behavior user guide defines behavioral risk, and what the requirement has internal auditors assess in an organization's approach to it.
questions.correct_explanation: The Organizational Behavior Topical Requirement has internal auditors assess whether the organization's approach to behavioral risk covers the behaviors its objectives depend on, and the user guide ties behavioral risk to objectives, not to rules alone. Engineers who rarely challenge a repair call break nothing, yet errors can reach aircraft, so a process blind to that habit is incomplete. The closest choice waits for a survey, but the gap is in what the process covers.

wrong_explanations.A: The user guide ties behavioral risk to the organization's objectives; misconduct and breaches are only part of it, and behavior measured against regulatory rules it calls conduct.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: a survey can show how far the pattern runs, which bears on its significance; the gap exists already, because the process is built to miss such behavior.
wrong_explanations.D: A hotline is a reporting channel the requirement covers separately; it does not set which behaviors the airline's objectives need, so the process's blind spot remains.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the user guide measures behavioral risk against objectives, not only rules, and D, because a hotline is a reporting channel, not the process's view of the behaviors needed.
Final two: B beats C because the gap is in the process's design, which leaves out behavior that breaks no rule; a survey would size this pattern, not reveal the gap.
Exam cue: on CIA questions about organizational behavior, measure behavior against the organization's objectives; a clean record of rule breaches does not show behavioral risk is managed.

questions.subtopic: 1C2 Culture and the control environment. A formal driver among four findings
questions.question: Reviewing second-nurse medicine checks at a district hospital, an internal auditor logs four findings. Which finding does the Organizational Behavior user guide best class as a formal driver of behavior?

options.A: Night nurses sign the check form with no second nurse present.
options.B: The hospital's quality report shows medicine errors up a fifth.
options.C: Nurses widely read the written check rule as a sign of distrust.
options.D: Ward targets count rounds finished on time, not checks completed.

questions.key_concept: Formal drivers are mechanisms the organization sets, such as targets; shared beliefs are informal drivers, even about written rules; behavior and outcomes are neither.
questions.pre_read: Recall how the Organizational Behavior user guide splits culture into behavior and what drives it, and how it splits the drivers.
questions.correct_explanation: In the Organizational Behavior user guide, culture is behavior plus its drivers, of two kinds: formal mechanisms such as targets, incentives and roles, and informal ones such as values and beliefs staff share. A ward target that rewards rounds finished on time is a goal the hospital set, so it is a formal driver. The closest choice concerns a written rule, but the nurses' view of it is a belief, an informal driver.

wrong_explanations.A: This is the behavior itself, though it involves a hospital form: an observable choice nurses make on rounds, which the drivers help to explain.
wrong_explanations.B: This is an outcome, though the hospital records it: a result the skipped checks may help produce, which the user guide keeps apart from behavior and drivers.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the written rule itself is a formal driver, as policies are, but this finding is the nurses' shared view of it, a belief and so an informal driver.

tips: Eliminate: A, because signing the form unchecked is still the behavior itself, and B, because a rise in recorded errors is an outcome the behavior may produce.
Final two: D beats C because a target is a goal the hospital sets, a formal driver; a belief nurses share stays informal even when it concerns a written rule.
Exam cue: on CIA culture questions, sort each finding by what it is, not by whether it touches a document: behavior, a driver or an outcome.
